title: Management: Everyday Manners
notes: Foundations course video for puppy and obedience owners (not reactivity). Claude drafted all narration from Tori's brief (Nov 24); the Google Doc is the source of truth. Build with LESSON=lesson-everyday.json.

beats.say: Hi, I’m Tori Ganino with Calling All Dogs. Welcome to Management: Everyday Manners.

scenes.heading: Where we're headed
scenes.visual_concept: Plan slide: What you'll learn, Why it matters.

beats.say: In this section, we’ll look at why management matters, how practice shapes your dog’s brain, and how to manage five everyday situations: greetings at the door, mealtime, jumping for things in your hands, pulling on walks, and barking at people.
Get this right, and the manners you teach will actually stick.

scenes.heading: Practice makes perfect
scenes.visual_concept: Tori's boxer picture; green chips for wanted habits, red chips for unwanted ones; callout.

beats.say: Every time your puppy or dog does something, they’re practicing it. And what gets practiced gets better.
That’s true for the things we love, like sitting politely or coming when called.
And it’s just as true for the things we don’t want.
Your dog isn’t being bad. They’re doing what works for them. And every time it works, they’re more likely to do it again.

scenes.heading: Building pathways
scenes.visual_concept: Brain picture: the old pathway in red; a path in the woods wears in; the new pathway in green.

beats.say: Here’s what’s happening in the brain. Every time your dog does a behavior, the neural pathway in the brain gets stronger.
beats.show: Brain picture; old pathway lights up.
beats.onscreen: The neural pathway in the brain gets stronger

beats.say: Think of a path in the woods. The first time, it’s barely visible. The more it’s walked, the easier it is to follow.
beats.show: Path in the woods wears in.

beats.say: Puppies are building these paths every day. The paths used most often become their habits.
beats.show: Row: the most walked paths become habits.
beats.onscreen: The paths used most often become habits

beats.say: So the goal is simple: keep your dog off the old path, and help them develop a new one.
beats.onscreen: Off the old path, develop a new one

scenes.heading: Management and training
scenes.visual_concept: Two cards: Management (prevents practice), Training (builds the new behavior); banner.

beats.say: That’s where management comes in. Management means setting up your dog’s world so they can’t practice the behavior you don’t want.
Training is the other half. It teaches your dog what to do instead, and makes that choice worth it.
Management stops the old habit from getting stronger. Training builds the new one. You need both.

scenes.heading: The foundation
scenes.visual_concept: Tori's house: the foundation, floors build up (new behaviors), a crack opens and the house shifts; callout.

beats.say: Think of it like building a house. Management is the foundation. Training builds the floors on top of it.
Every new behavior you teach, like sitting at the door, waiting for the bowl, or walking on a loose leash, is another floor.
beats.onscreen: Sit at the door, Wait for the bowl, Loose leash walking

beats.say: But if the foundation has a crack, everything you build on it starts to shift. Every time your dog practices what you don’t want, that’s a crack.
Keep the foundation solid, and the new behaviors you teach will hold.

scenes.heading: Everyone follows the plan
scenes.visual_concept: Every time + Every person; red callout; four people cards.

beats.say: Management only works if everyone follows it, every time.
If one person lets the puppy jump up for a hug, or slips food from the table, your dog learns the rule is optional.
So get the whole household on the same page: family, kids, guests, dog walkers, and sitters.
beats.onscreen: Family, Kids, Guests, Walkers and sitters

scenes.heading: Teach what you want instead
scenes.visual_concept: Two cards: What you don't want (red, a crossed 'No!') vs What you want (green, a clear picture); context chips; preview of the three blocks.

beats.say: Before we look at each situation, one rule applies to all of them. You need a clear picture of what you want your dog to do, not just what you don’t want them to do.
beats.onscreen: A clear picture of what you want

beats.say: Just telling your dog no isn’t fair. They need to learn that there are other options, ones we prefer, and that those choices pay off.
Then practice those choices in lots of different places and situations, so your dog really understands them wherever you are.
For each situation, we’ll look at what your dog practices, how to manage it, and some examples of what you can teach instead.
beats.onscreen: What they practice, Manage it, Teach instead

scenes.heading: Greetings at the door
scenes.visual_concept: Situation slide: the golden jumping on a guest; the greeting ritual loop; Manage it; Teach instead examples while Tori's dachshund clip (jumping, then four paws on the floor) plays muted in the picture's place.

beats.say: Let’s start at the front door. A guest walks in, and your dog jumps all over them.
This can turn into a greeting ritual. Your dog jumps, the person asks for a sit, your dog sits, and then gets attention. Now the jump is part of the routine.
beats.onscreen: Jumps, Asked to sit, Sits, Gets attention

beats.say: Manage it so the jump never becomes part of the ritual. Put up a baby gate or clip on a leash before you open the door, so your dog can’t reach your guest.
beats.onscreen: Baby gate or leash, before the door opens

beats.say: Then teach what you want instead. For example, four paws on the floor, like this little dachshund is learning, or going to a mat. Reward that calm hello.
beats.show: Teach instead; the dachshund clip plays muted in the picture's place.
beats.onscreen: For example: four paws on the floor, or go to a mat

scenes.heading: Mealtime
scenes.visual_concept: Situation slide: picture placeholder (mealtime); four red chips; Manage it rows; Teach instead example.

beats.say: Next, food. Counter surfing, mugging you or grabbing food from your hands, jumping up while you make their meal, guarding the bowl. Every time it pays off, it gets stronger.
beats.onscreen: Counter surfing, Mugging and grabbing, Jumping at meal prep, Guarding the bowl

beats.say: Manage it by keeping food off the counters and out of reach, and by using a gate, crate, or mat while you make meals and while you eat.
beats.onscreen: Food out of reach; gate, crate, or mat during meals

beats.say: If your dog guards the bowl, give them a quiet spot to eat in peace, with no one hovering or reaching in. If it’s getting worse, reach out for help.
beats.onscreen: A quiet spot to eat in peace

beats.say: Then teach what you want your dog to do instead, like settling on a mat while you cook.

scenes.heading: Jumping for things in hands
scenes.visual_concept: Situation slide: picture placeholder; Practicing / Manage it (out of reach; baby gate for the groceries) / Teach instead examples.

beats.say: Then there’s jumping up for whatever’s in your hands: food, toys, the mail. If jumping gets them the thing even once, they’ll try again, and harder.
beats.onscreen: Jumping for food, toys, the mail

beats.say: Manage it by keeping things up and out of reach. If you’re carrying in the groceries and your dog can’t handle that excitement, have your dog behind a baby gate.
beats.onscreen: Out of reach; a baby gate for the groceries

beats.say: Then teach what you want instead. For example, a sit or four paws on the floor, and that calm choice earns the toy or the treat.
beats.onscreen: For example: a sit, or four paws on the floor

scenes.heading: Pulling on walks
scenes.visual_concept: Situation slide: Practicing / Manage it (harness, head halter once conditioned) / Teach instead; the loose leash walking clip plays muted in a tall frame at right.

beats.say: On walks, every time your dog pulls and gets where they want to go, pulling works. Do that every day, and it becomes how they walk.
Manage it with a well fitted harness. A head halter can help too, as long as your dog has been properly conditioned to wear it.
Then teach what you want instead, like walking on a loose leash, the way this dog is doing, and reward your dog for walking next to you.

scenes.heading: Barking at people
scenes.visual_concept: Situation slide: picture at right (golden barking at a man through the window); reasons; manage it; ABCs course card.

beats.say: And finally, barking at people, at the window or out on walks.
Dogs bark at people for different reasons. Sometimes they really want that person to come closer. And when the person comes over, or the barking gets attention, it works.
beats.onscreen: They want the person to come closer

beats.say: Manage it by blocking the view at the window, with film or closed blinds, and by giving people space on walks before your dog starts barking.
beats.onscreen: Block the view; give people space

beats.say: Why your dog barks matters, because it changes how we train. We cover that in our ABCs of Behavior course.

scenes.heading: “Just this once”
scenes.visual_concept: Just this once chips drop one by one, each adding a rep on the old path (red meter); callout.

beats.say: It’s easy to think, just this once won’t hurt. A quick jump for a hug, one bite from the table.
But your dog doesn’t know it’s just this once. To them, it’s one more rep on the old path.
beats.onscreen: One more rep on the old path

beats.say: Small slips add up. Being consistent is what makes new manners stick.

scenes.heading: Bringing it together
scenes.visual_concept: Level house on its foundation; three takeaways; closing statement (no logo close: the assignment comes next).

beats.say: Let’s bring it together. What your dog practices, they get better at. Management keeps the unwanted behaviors from being practiced.
Training teaches what to do instead, and everyone in your home follows the same plan.
Management is the foundation. Build on a strong foundation, one without cracks from management slipping, and the manners you teach will last.

scenes.heading: Your assignment
scenes.visual_concept: A worksheet: three columns (Behavior I don't want / When and where it happens / How I'll manage it), one example row fills in; two numbered steps; logo close.

beats.say: Now it’s your turn. Here’s your assignment.
First, make a list of the behaviors you don’t want to continue, and the situations they happen in. Be specific. Not just jumping, but jumping on guests when they come through the front door.
beats.show: Step 1; example row: behavior and situation.
beats.onscreen: List the behaviors and the situations. Be specific.

beats.say: Then, for each one, look at what you can do to manage the environment temporarily, so those behaviors can’t get practiced while you’re teaching new ones.
beats.show: Step 2; example row: how I'll manage it; logo close.
